title: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)
hook: each tribal leader brings an identical gift, and each is listed in full

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Kohanim: three lines that grow from three words to seven, and end in peace. Your line was bless thee, and keep thee. Today, the end of Naso.

At a graduation, the dean reads every single name. Three hundred students, and each one walks across the stage, shakes the same hand, takes the same rolled-up paper. It takes forever. Somebody in the back row checks their phone. Wouldn't it be faster to say congratulations, everyone? Sure. But ask any parent in the audience whether it's the same. Numbers chapter seven makes the slow choice on purpose, twelve times in a row, and the chapter grows long because of it.
screen: `EVERY NAME READ ALOUD.` → `THE SAME HANDSHAKE, 300 TIMES.` → `THE SLOW CHOICE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The Tabernacle is finished and anointed, and the leaders of the twelve tribes come forward to dedicate the altar. Each leader is called a nasi, from the same root as naso: one who is lifted up. They bring their gifts one per day, for twelve days. On the first day, Nachshon, of Judah: one silver dish and one silver basin, both full of fine flour mixed with oil; one golden pan full of incense; a bull, a ram, a lamb, a goat, and more for the peace offerings. On the second day, the leader of Issachar brings exactly the same. And the third. Down to the shekel. And the Torah writes it out every time: twelve paragraphs, almost word for word, then a grand total. Eighty-nine verses. An editor might cut it. The commentators asked why it stays. Nachmanides answers that God wanted to honor each leader equally. Each chose to bring the gift on his own day, and the Torah wouldn't let anyone be summarized as the same as the one before. A midrash goes further: the gifts were identical, but each leader had his own meaning in mind, tied to his own tribe's story. Same silver, different hearts. This chapter is also read in synagogue during Hanukkah, because its theme is dedication. The Hebrew for dedication of the altar is chanukat hamizbe'ach. Hanukkah is the same word.
screen: `NASI: ONE LIFTED UP.` · `TWELVE DAYS, ONE IDENTICAL GIFT.` · `EACH ONE WRITTEN OUT IN FULL.` · `SAME SILVER, DIFFERENT HEARTS.` · then, large: `EACH GIFT COUNTED IN FULL.`

segments.voice: Think of a good thing lots of people around you do so often it blurs: the parents who all pack lunches, the nurses on the night shift, the volunteers who show up every Sunday. Pick out one of them and give them their own paragraph in your mind: their name, their face, the way they do it. Then another, without summarizing.
Naso, the portion of lifting, closing with twelve identical gifts, each one written out in full.
Your line: each gift counted in full. No one is just one of the twelve. See you tomorrow.
